passage_1.text:
Octopuses are misfits in their own extended families. They belong to the Mollusca class Cephalopoda. But they don't look like their cousins at all. Other molluscs include sea snails, sea slugs, bivalves – most are shelled invertebrates with a dorsal foot. Cephalopods are all arms, and can be as tiny as 1 centimetre and as large at 30 feet. Some of them have brains the size of a walnut, which is large for an invertebrate.

It makes sense for these molluscs to have added protection in the form of a higher cognition; they don't have a shell covering them, and pretty much everything feeds on cephalopods, including humans. But how did cephalopods manage to secure their own invisibility cloak? Cephalopods fire from multiple cylinders to achieve this in varying degrees from species to species. There are four main catalysts - chromatophores, iridophores, papillae and leucophores.

Chromatophores are organs on their bodies that contain pigment sacs, which have red, yellow and brown pigment granules. These sacs have a network of radial muscles, meaning muscles arranged in a circle radiating outwards. These are connected to the brain by a nerve. When the cephalopod wants to change colour, the brain carries an electrical impulse through the nerve to the muscles that expand outwards, pulling open the sacs to display the colours on the skin. Why these three colours? Because these are the colours the light reflects at the depths they live in (the rest is absorbed before it reaches those depths).

Well, what about other colours? Cue the iridophores. Think of a second level of skin that has thin stacks of cells. These can reflect light back at different wavelengths. It's using the same properties that we've seen in hologram stickers, or rainbows on puddles of oil. You move your head and you see a different colour. The sticker isn't doing anything but reflecting light – it's your movement that's changing the appearance of the colour. This property of holograms, oil and other such surfaces is called "iridescence".

Papillae are sections of the skin that can be deformed to make a texture bumpy. Even humans possess them (goosebumps) but cannot use them in the manner that cephalopods can. For instance, the use of these cells is how an octopus can wrap itself over a rock and appear jagged or how a squid or cuttlefish can imitate the look of a coral reef by growing miniature towers on its skin. It actually matches the texture of the substrate it chooses.

Finally, the leucophores: According to a paper, published in Nature, cuttlefish and octopuses possess an additional type of reflector cell called a leucophore. They are cells that scatter full spectrum light so that they appear white in a similar way that a polar bear's fur appears white. Leucophores will also reflect any filtered light shown on them. If the water appears blue at a certain depth, the octopuses and cuttlefish can appear blue; if the water appears green, they appear green, and so on and so forth.

passage_2.text:
When we teach engineering problems now, we ask students to come to a single "best" solution defined by technical ideals like low cost, speed to build, and ability to scale. This way of teaching primes students to believe that their decision-making is purely objective, as it is grounded in math and science. This is known as technical-social dualism, the idea that the technical and social dimensions of engineering problems are readily separable and remain distinct throughout the problem-definition and solution process.

Nontechnical parameters such as access to a technology, cultural relevancy or potential harms are deemed political and invalid in this way of learning. But those technical ideals are at their core social and political choices determined by a dominant culture focused on economic growth for the most privileged segments of society. By choosing to downplay public welfare as a critical parameter for engineering design, we risk creating a culture of disengagement from societal concerns amongst engineers that is antithetical to the ethical code of engineering.

In my field of medical devices, ignoring social dimensions has real consequences. Most FDA-approved drugs are incorrectly dosed for people assigned female at birth, leading to unexpected adverse reactions. This is because they have been inadequately represented in clinical trials.

Beyond physical failings, subjective beliefs treated as facts by those in decision-making roles can encode social inequities. For example, spirometers, routinely used devices that measure lung capacity, still have correction factors that automatically assume smaller lung capacity in Black and Asian individuals. These racially based adjustments are derived from research done by eugenicists who thought these racial differences were biologically determined and who considered nonwhite people as inferior. These machines ignore the influence of social and environmental factors on lung capacity.

Many technologies for systemically marginalized people have not been built because they were not deemed important such as better early diagnostics and treatment for diseases like endometriosis, a disease that afflicts 10 percent of people with uteruses. And we hardly question whether devices are built sustainably, which has led to a crisis of medical waste and health care accounting for 10 percent of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions.

Social justice must be made core to the way engineers are trained. Some universities are working on this. Engineers taught this way will be prepared to think critically about what problems we choose to solve, how we do so responsibly and how we build teams that challenge our ways of thinking.

Individual engineering professors are also working to embed societal needs in their pedagogy. Darshan Karwat at the University of Arizona developed activist engineering to challenge engineers to acknowledge their full moral and social responsibility through practical self- reflection. Khalid Kadir at the University of California, Berkeley, created the popular course Engineering, Environment, and Society that teaches engineers how to engage in place-based knowledge, an understanding of the people, context and history, to design better technical approaches in collaboration with communities. When we design and build with equity and justice in mind, we craft better solutions that respond to the complexities of entrenched systemic problems.

passage_3.text:
Humans today make music. Think beyond all the qualifications that might trail after this bald statement: that only certain humans make music, that extensive training is involved, that many societies distinguish musical specialists from nonmusicians, that in today's societies most listen to music rather than making it, and so forth. These qualifications, whatever their local merit, are moot in the face of the overarching truth that making music, considered from a cognitive and psychological vantage, is the province of all those who perceive and experience what is made. We are, almost all of us, musicians – everyone who can entrain (not necessarily dance) to a beat, who can recognize a repeated tune (not necessarily sing it), who can distinguish one instrument or one singing voice from another. I will often use an antique word, recently revived, to name this broader musical experience. Humans are musicking creatures.

The set of capacities that enables musicking is a principal marker of modern humanity. There is nothing polemical in this assertion except a certain insistence, which will figure often in what follows, that musicking be included in our thinking about fundamental human commonalities. Capacities involved in musicking are many and take shape in complicated ways, arising from innate dispositions. Most of these capacities overlap with nonmusical ones, though a few may be distinct and dedicated to musical perception and production. In the area of overlap, linguistic capacities seem to be particularly important, and humans are (in principle) language- makers in addition to music-makers – speaking creatures as well as musicking ones.

Humans are symbol-makers too, a feature tightly bound up with language, not so tightly with music. The species Cassirer dubbed Homo symbolicus cannot help but tangle musicking in webs of symbolic thought and expression, habitually making it a component of behavioral complexes that form such expression. But in fundamental features musicking is neither language- like nor symbol-like, and from these differences come many clues to its ancient emergence.

If musicking is a primary, shared trait of modern humans, then to describe its emergence must be to detail the coalescing of that modernity. This took place, archaeologists are clear, over a very long durée: at least 50,000 years or so, more likely something closer to 200,000, depending in part on what that coalescence is taken to comprise. If we look back 20,000 years, a small portion of this long period, we reach the lives of humans whose musical capacities were probably little different from our own. As we look farther back we reach horizons where this similarity can no longer hold – perhaps 40,000 years ago, perhaps 70,000, perhaps 100,000. But we never cross a line before which all the cognitive capacities recruited in modern musicking abruptly disappear. Unless we embrace the incredible notion that music sprang forth in full-blown glory, its emergence will have to be tracked in gradualist terms across a long period.

This is one general feature of a history of music's emergence. The history was at once sociocultural and biological. The capacities recruited in musicking are many, so describing its emergence involves following several or many separate strands.

passage_4.text:
We begin with the emergence of the philosophy of the social sciences as an arena of thought and as a set of social institutions. The two characterisations overlap but are not congruent. Academic disciplines are social institutions. My view is that institutions are all those social entities that organise action: they link acting individuals into social structures. There are various kinds of institutions. Hegelians and Marxists emphasise universal institutions such as the family, rituals, governance, economy and the military. These are mostly institutions that just grew. Perhaps in some imaginary beginning of time they spontaneously appeared. In their present incarnations, however, they are very much the product of conscious attempts to mould and plan them. We have family law, established and disestablished churches, constitutions and laws, including those governing the economy and the military. Institutions deriving from statute, like joint-stock companies are formal by contrast with informal ones such as friendships. There are some institutions that come in both informal and formal variants, as well as in mixed ones. Consider the fact that the stock exchange and the black market are both market institutions, one formal one not. Consider further that there are many features of the work of the stock exchange that rely on informal, noncodifiable agreements, not least the language used for communication. To be precise, mixtures are the norm. From constitutions at the top to by-laws near the bottom we are always adding to, or tinkering with, earlier institutions, the grown and the designed are intertwined.

It is usual in social thought to treat culture and tradition as different from, although alongside, institutions. The view taken here is different. Culture and tradition are sub-sets of institutions analytically isolated for explanatory or expository purposes. Some social scientists have taken all institutions, even purely local ones, to be entities that satisfy basic human needs under local conditions. Others differed and declared any structure of reciprocal roles and norms an institution. Most of these differences are differences of emphasis rather than disagreements. Let us straddle all these versions and present institutions very generally as structures that serve to coordinate the actions of individuals. Institutions themselves then have no aims or purpose other than those given to them by actors or used by actors to explain them.

Language is the formative institution for social life and for science. Both formal and informal language is involved, naturally grown or designed. (Language is all of these to varying degrees.) Languages are paradigms of institutions or, from another perspective, nested sets of institutions. Syntax, semantics, lexicon and alphabet/character-set are all institutions within the larger institutional framework of a written language. Natural languages are typical examples of what Ferguson called 'the result of human action, but not the execution of any human design; reformed natural languages and artificial languages introduce design into their modifications or refinements of natural language. Above all, languages are paradigms of institutional tools that function to coordinate.

questions.question_text: All of the following are reasons for octopuses being "misfits" EXCEPT that they:

options.label: A
options.text: exhibit higher intelligence than other molluscs.

options.label: B
options.text: have several arms.

options.label: C
options.text: are consumed by humans and other animals.

options.label: D
options.text: do not possess an outer protective shell.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what doesn't make octopuses different or "misfit" among their extended family of molluscs.

The key is understanding what makes something a "misfit" -> it has to be different from the group. So I'm looking for something that octopuses share with other molluscs or cephalopods.

From passage: "Octopuses are misfits in their own extended families. They belong to the Mollusca class Cephalopoda. But they don't look like their cousins at all."

The passage explains octopuses are different because -> other molluscs are "shelled invertebrates with a dorsal foot" but cephalopods are "all arms" and don't have shells.

From passage: "pretty much everything feeds on cephalopods, including humans"

This line is crucial -> it says all cephalopods (not just octopuses) are eaten by humans and other animals.

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> Higher intelligence does make them misfits because passage says they have "brains the size of a walnut, which is large for an invertebrate" compared to other molluscs

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> Having arms makes them misfits because other molluscs have "a dorsal foot" while "cephalopods are all arms"

🟢 Option 3 is correct -> This is shared by all cephalopods, not unique to octopuses. The passage says "everything feeds on cephalopods" - so being eaten doesn't make octopuses different from their cephalopod cousins

🟠 Option 4 -> partial-truth -> Not having shells makes them misfits because "most" other molluscs "are shelled invertebrates" but cephalopods "don't have a shell covering them"

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements is not true about the camouflaging ability of Cephalopods?

options.label: A
options.text: Cephalopods can change their colour.

options.label: B
options.text: Cephalopods can take on the colour of their predator.

options.label: C
options.text: Cephalopods can change their texture.

options.label: D
options.text: Cephalopods can blend into the colour of their surroundings.

questions.explanation_text:
The passage explains four ways cephalopods camouflage: chromatophores (color organs), iridophores (light reflection), papillae (texture change), and leucophores (matching water colors).

From passage: "Leucophores will also reflect any filtered light shown on them. If the water appears blue at a certain depth, the octopuses and cuttlefish can appear blue; if the water appears green, they appear green"

Key insight -> The passage talks about matching surroundings and environment, not predators specifically.

🟢 Option 1 -> clearly supported -> chromatophores contain pigments that display colors on skin

🔴 Option 2 -> not mentioned in passage -> talks about matching water colors, substrate textures, surroundings - but never mentions copying predator colors specifically

🟢 Option 3 -> directly supported -> papillae can "deform to make texture bumpy" and match substrate texture

🟢 Option 4 -> clearly supported -> leucophores reflect filtered light colors from surroundings, making them blend in

The confusion here might be thinking "predators are part of surroundings" -> but the passage is specific about what they copy: water colors, substrate textures, coral reef appearance. It never mentions predator mimicry.

questions.question_text: Based on the passage, it can be inferred that camouflaging techniques in an octopus are most dissimilar to those in:

options.label: A
options.text: sea snails

options.label: B
options.text: cuttlefish

options.label: C
options.text: polar bears

options.label: D
options.text: squids

questions.explanation_text:
Need to compare octopus camouflage with each option.

From passage: "They belong to the Mollusca class Cephalopoda. But they don't look like their cousins at all. Other molluscs include sea snails, sea slugs, bivalves – most are shelled invertebrates with a dorsal foot."

From passage: "It makes sense for these molluscs to have added protection in the form of a higher cognition; they don't have a shell covering them"

Octopuses use advanced camouflage -> chromatophores, iridophores, papillae, leucophores -> because they have no shell for protection.

Other molluscs like sea snails -> have shells for protection -> don't need fancy camouflage tricks.

Elimination Process:

🟢 Option 1: Sea snails -> most dissimilar -> Sea snails are molluscs but not cephalopods. They have shells for protection, so they don't need the fancy camouflage tricks that octopuses use.

🔴 Option 2: Cuttlefish -> very similar -> Passage says "cuttlefish and octopuses possess leucophores" - they're both cephalopods with same camouflage methods.

🔴 Option 3: Polar bears -> only mentioned as example -> Just used to explain how leucophores look white, not about actual camouflage techniques.

🔴 Option 4: Squids -> very similar -> Passage mentions squids can "imitate coral reef by growing miniature towers" using papillae - same camouflage methods as octopuses.

Key insight: Cuttlefish and squids are fellow cephalopods -> share same camouflage toolkit. Sea snails rely on shells instead of color-changing tricks -> most different approach.

questions.question_text: Based on the passage, we can infer that all of the following statements, if true, would weaken the camouflaging adeptness of Cephalopods EXCEPT

options.label: A
options.text: the hydrostatic pressure at the depths at which Cephalopods reside renders radial muscle movements difficult.

options.label: B
options.text: the temperature of water at the depths at which Cephalopods reside renders the transmission of neural signals difficult.

options.label: C
options.text: light reflects the colours red, green, and yellow at the depths at which Cephalopods reside.

options.label: D
options.text: the number of chromatophores in Cephalopods is half the number of iridophores and leucophores.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which statement would NOT weaken cephalopod camouflaging. Let us trace through how their camouflaging works first.

From passage: "There are four main catalysts - chromatophores, iridophores, papillae and leucophores."

The passage explains cephalopods use multiple systems -> chromatophores (color-changing organs controlled by brain signals and radial muscles) + iridophores (reflect light like holograms) + papillae (texture changes) + leucophores (white light reflection).

So anything that disrupts these core mechanisms would weaken their camouflaging ability.

🔴 Option 1 -> directly disrupts core mechanism -> If radial muscles can't move properly due to pressure, chromatophores can't expand to show colors. This clearly weakens camouflaging.

🔴 Option 2 -> directly disrupts core mechanism -> If neural signals can't transmit properly, the brain can't control chromatophores. This clearly weakens camouflaging.

🔴 Option 3 -> creates color mismatch -> Passage says chromatophores have "red, yellow and brown pigment granules" that match light colors at their depths. If light reflects green instead of brown, they can't match properly. This weakens camouflaging.

🟢 Option 4 -> just describes cell ratios -> Having fewer chromatophores but still having iridophores and leucophores means they still possess multiple functioning camouflage systems. The ratio doesn't eliminate any mechanism - all tools are still available, just in different amounts.

Think of it this way: Options 1-3 break or disrupt the camouflaging tools, but Option 4 just changes how many of each tool they have -> the tools themselves still work perfectly fine.

questions.question_text: In this passage, the author is making the claim that:

options.label: A
options.text: the objective of best solutions in engineering has shifted the focus of pedagogy from humanism and social obligations to technological perfection.

options.label: B
options.text: engineering students today are trained to be non-subjective in their reasoning as this best enables them to develop much-needed universal solutions.

options.label: C
options.text: technical-social dualism has emerged as a technique for engineering students to incorporate social considerations into their technical problem-solving processes.

options.label: D
options.text: engineering students today are taught to focus on objective technical outcomes, independent of the social dimensions of their work.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "When we teach engineering problems now, we ask students to come to a single 'best' solution defined by technical ideals like low cost, speed to build, and ability to scale. This way of teaching primes students to believe that their decision-making is purely objective"

The author is critiquing current engineering education -> They describe what's wrong with it -> They explain how students are currently being taught -> This creates problems in the real world

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> talks about a historical "shift" from humanism to tech perfection, but the passage doesn't discuss any historical change - it just describes the current problematic state

🔴 Option 2 -> context-shift -> sounds like it's praising current training ("this best enables them"), but the author is actually criticizing current methods throughout the passage

🔴 Option 3 -> complete reversal -> says technical-social dualism helps students "incorporate social considerations," but the passage clearly states it does the opposite - it separates and excludes social dimensions

🟢 Option 4 -> correct -> perfectly captures the author's main claim about current education - students ARE taught to focus only on technical outcomes while ignoring social dimensions

The key insight: The author isn't praising anything or talking about historical changes. They're making a straightforward claim about what's currently happening in engineering education that they think is wrong.

From passage: "Nontechnical parameters such as access to a technology, cultural relevancy or potential harms are deemed political and invalid in this way of learning"

Option 4 directly states the problematic approach the author identifies -> Students focus on objective technical outcomes -> They ignore social dimensions -> This is exactly what the author says is happening now.

questions.question_text: The author gives all of the following reasons for why marginalised people are systematically discriminated against in technology-related interventions EXCEPT

options.label: A
options.text: "But those technical ideals are at their core social and political choices determined by a dominant culture focused on economic growth for the most privileged segments of society."

options.label: B
options.text: "Beyond physical failings, subjective beliefs treated as facts by those in decision-making roles can encode social inequities."

options.label: C
options.text: "And we hardly question whether devices are built sustainably, which has led to a crisis of medical waste and health care accounting for 10 percent of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions."

options.label: D
options.text: "These racially based adjustments are derived from research done by eugenicists who thought these racial differences were biologically determined and who considered nonwhite people as inferior."

questions.explanation_text:
Need to identify which quote talks about something else entirely.

From passage: "And we hardly question whether devices are built sustainably, which has led to a crisis of medical waste and health care accounting for 10 percent of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions."

The passage gives several examples of discrimination -> but one quote is about a different problem entirely -> environmental impact affects everyone equally, not specifically marginalized groups.

🟠 Option 1 -> discrimination example -> talks about dominant culture favoring "most privileged segments" -> clearly shows marginalized people being left out

🟠 Option 2 -> discrimination example -> mentions "decision-makers" creating "social inequities" -> shows how bias against marginalized groups happens

🟢 Option 3 is correct -> environmental concern -> talks about waste and emissions affecting everyone equally -> nothing about targeting or ignoring marginalized people specifically

🟠 Option 4 -> discrimination example -> mentions "eugenicists" who considered "nonwhite people as inferior" -> obvious discrimination against racial minorities

The key insight: Options 1, 2, and 4 all explain how marginalized people face discrimination through biased decision-making, historical prejudice, or being ignored by privileged groups. Option 3 discusses environmental problems that affect everyone regardless of social status.

questions.question_text: All of the following are examples of the negative outcomes of focusing on technical ideals in the medical sphere EXCEPT the:

options.label: A
options.text: neglect of research and development of medical technologies for the diagnosis and treatment of diseases that typically afflict marginalised communities.

options.label: B
options.text: exclusion of non-privileged groups in clinical trials which leads to incorrect drug dosages.

options.label: C
options.text: incorrect assignment of people as female at birth which has resulted in faulty drug interventions.

options.label: D
options.text: continuing calibration of medical devices based on past racial biases that have remained unadjusted for changes.

questions.explanation_text:
Let us trace through the passage to find what problems it actually mentions:

From passage: "Most FDA-approved drugs are incorrectly dosed for people assigned female at birth, leading to unexpected adverse reactions. This is because they have been inadequately represented in clinical trials."

From passage: "spirometers, routinely used devices that measure lung capacity, still have correction factors that automatically assume smaller lung capacity in Black and Asian individuals"

From passage: "Many technologies for systemically marginalized people have not been built because they were not deemed important such as better early diagnostics and treatment for diseases like endometriosis"

The passage shows clear problems: drugs dosed wrong -> inadequate representation in trials -> devices using racist assumptions -> neglecting marginalized diseases.

Nowwe need to check which option doesn't match what the passage actually says:

🟠 Option 1 -> matches passage -> endometriosis example shows neglect of marginalized communities' medical needs

🟠 Option 2 -> matches passage -> clinical trial exclusion leading to wrong drug doses for people assigned female at birth

🔴 Option 3 -> misreads passage -> passage talks about people who were correctly assigned female at birth but inadequately represented in trials, not "incorrect assignment"

🟠 Option 4 -> matches passage -> spirometer racial bias example shows devices using outdated racist assumptions

The key confusion: Option 3 twists the passage. The passage says people assigned female at birth get wrong drug doses because they weren't included enough in trials. It's not saying they were incorrectly assigned female at birth - that's a completely different issue not mentioned in the passage.

questions.question_text: We can infer that the author would approve of a more evolved engineering pedagogy that includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: making considerations of environmental sustainability intrinsic to the development of technological solutions.

options.label: B
options.text: moving towards technical-social dualism where social community needs are incorporated in problem-definition and solutions.

options.label: C
options.text: design that is based on the needs of communities using local knowledge and responding to local priorities.

options.label: D
options.text: a more responsible approach to technical design and problem-solving than a focus on speed in developing and bringing to scale.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the author would NOT approve of in better engineering teaching. This means finding the option that goes against the author's main ideas.

From passage: "This is known as technical-social dualism, the idea that the technical and social dimensions of engineering problems are readily separable and remain distinct throughout the problem-definition and solution process."

The author clearly opposes technical-social dualism -> says it's the root problem -> wants technical and social parts combined, not separated -> this creates the harmful "purely objective" thinking that ignores social impacts.

Author's solution -> integrate social justice into engineering training -> don't separate technical from social -> consider equity, community needs, environmental impact together.

Elimination process:

🟢 Option 1 -> correct match -> author directly supports environmental concerns, mentions medical waste crisis and healthcare's 10% of greenhouse gas emissions

🔴 Option 2 -> contradicts author's core argument -> author wants to eliminate technical-social dualism entirely, not move toward it. Even though it mentions incorporating social needs, keeping dualism contradicts the author's main point

🟢 Option 3 -> perfect match -> author specifically praises Khalid Kadir's work on "place-based knowledge" and designing "in collaboration with communities"

🟢 Option 4 -> clear support -> author criticizes current focus on "speed to build" as one of the harmful technical ideals that ignore social welfare

The confusion might be that Option 2 mentions incorporating social needs, which sounds good. But the key word is "dualism" -> the author wants integration, not separation with add-ons.

Answer: Option 2

The author completely rejects technical-social dualism as the core problem in engineering education. Moving toward dualism, even with social considerations, still maintains the harmful separation the author wants to eliminate.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following sets of terms best serves as keywords to the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: Humans; Musicking; Linguistic capacities; Symbol-making; Modern humanity.

options.label: B
options.text: Musicking; Cognitive psychology; Antique; Symbol-makers; Modernity.

options.label: C
options.text: Humans; Psychological vantage; Musicking; Cassirer; Emergence of music.

options.label: D
options.text: Humans; Capacities; Language; Symbols; Modernity

questions.explanation_text:
Let us trace what each paragraph focuses on:

Para 1 -> Humans are musicking creatures

Para 2 -> Musicking capacities of modern humanity, overlap with linguistic capacities

Para 3 -> Humans as symbol-makers, but musicking is different

Para 4 -> Modern humans and musicking emergence over time

Para 5 -> History of musicking emergence

From passage: "Humans are musicking creatures" and "musical capacities seem to be particularly important" and "Humans are symbol-makers too"

The passage consistently returns to: humans -> their musicking nature -> how it relates to language/symbols -> and what makes modern humanity special.

Here's how to eliminate wrong options by checking if they capture the core themes:

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> hits all major themes: Humans, Musicking, Linguistic capacities, Symbol-making, Modern humanity (covers every key concept)

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> has "Musicking" and "Symbol-makers" but misses Humans (the main subject). "Cognitive psychology" and "Antique" are minor mentions, not main themes

🟠 Option 3 -> scope-error -> includes "Humans" and "Musicking" but "Cassirer" is just one reference, not a keyword. Misses "linguistic capacities" and "symbol-making" which are major themes

🟠 Option 4 -> degree-error -> right direction but too vague. Says "Capacities" instead of the specific "Musicking" which is the central focus. "Language" is less precise than "linguistic capacities"

The trap: Options 2-4 have some correct terms but miss the specific focus on musicking or use terms that are too broad/minor.

questions.question_text: Based on the passage, which one of the following statements is a valid argument about the emergence of music/musicking?

options.label: A
options.text: ,000 years ago, human musical capacities were not very different from what they are today.

options.label: B
options.text: Anyone who can perceive and experience music must be considered capable of musicking.

options.label: C
options.text: All musical work is located in the overlap between linguistic capacity and music production.

options.label: D
options.text: Although musicking is not language-like, it shares the quality of being a form of expression.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "If we look back 20,000 years, a small portion of this long period, we reach the lives of humans whose musical capacities were probably little different from our own."

Key insight -> question asks specifically about emergence (how music developed) -> only one option talks about music's historical development -> others discuss current musicking abilities.

🟠 Option 2 -> scope-error -> correctly describes who can musick today but doesn't address emergence/history at all

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth + scope-error -> passage says linguistic capacities are "particularly important" in overlap areas, but also mentions some capacities may be "distinct and dedicated" to music, so not ALL musical work is in linguistic overlap. Also doesn't address emergence.

🟠 Option 4 -> scope-error -> discusses current nature of musicking (expression quality) but says nothing about how music emerged historically

🟢 Option 1 -> directly supported -> passage explicitly states humans 20,000 years ago had musical capacities "probably little different from our own" -> this IS an argument about emergence showing musical abilities were already well-developed by then

The passage gives a clear timeline -> 20,000 years ago = similar abilities to today -> this directly answers how music emerged (gradually over long period, with abilities already mature 20,000 years ago).

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements, if true, would weaken the author's claim that humans are musicking creatures?

options.label: A
options.text: Musical capacities are primarily socio-cultural, which explains the wide diversity of musical forms.

options.label: B
options.text: As musicking is neither language-like nor symbol-like, it is a much older form of expression.

options.label: C
options.text: Nonmusical capacities are of far greater consequence to human survival than the capacity for music.

options.label: D
options.text: From a cognitive and psychological vantage, musicking arises from unconscious dispositions, not conscious ones.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what would weaken the author's main claim that humans are "musicking creatures."

The author's core argument is that musicking is a universal, cognitive ability - not just cultural. Let us trace this:

From passage: "making music, considered from a cognitive and psychological vantage, is the province of all those who perceive and experience what is made"

From passage: "These qualifications, whatever their local merit, are moot in the face of the overarching truth"

Author's logic: Cultural differences don't matter -> Musicking is fundamentally cognitive -> All humans are musical creatures

So what would weaken this? Something that says musicking is primarily cultural, not cognitive.

🔴 Option 1 -> directly contradicts -> Says musical capacities are "primarily socio-cultural" which goes against author's "cognitive and psychological vantage" argument

🟢 Option 2 -> supports author -> Author already says musicking is "neither language-like nor symbol-like" and discusses its ancient emergence

🟠 Option 3 -> irrelevant scope -> Author never claims music is most important for survival, just that it's universal. This doesn't weaken the "musicking creatures" claim

🟠 Option 4 -> supports author -> Author mentions "innate dispositions" and emphasizes cognitive/psychological basis, so unconscious dispositions actually fit this view

The key confusion students might have: Option 3 seems to challenge music's importance. But the author isn't arguing music is the most important human trait - just that it's universal. Something being less important for survival doesn't make it less universal.

Option 1 attacks the foundation of the argument by saying musicking is primarily cultural (varies between societies) rather than cognitive (universal to all humans).

questions.question_text: "Think beyond all the qualifications that might trail after this bald statement " In the context of the passage, what is the author trying to communicate in this quoted extract?

options.label: A
options.text: A bald statement is one that is trailed by a series of qualifying clarifications and caveats.

options.label: B
options.text: Although there may be many caveats and other considerations, the statement is essentially true.

options.label: C
options.text: Thinking beyond qualifications allows us to give free reign to musical expressions.

options.label: D
options.text: A bald statement is one that requires no qualifications to infer its meaning.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to understand what the author means when they say "think beyond all the qualifications that might trail after this bald statement."

From passage: "These qualifications, whatever their local merit, are moot in the face of the overarching truth that making music... is the province of all those who perceive and experience what is made."

The author starts with the simple statement "Humans today make music" -> then lists all the ways people might limit or qualify this statement (only some humans, needs training, etc.) -> but then says these qualifications don't matter because the deeper truth is that ALL humans are musical creatures.

The key insight: Author acknowledges the qualifications exist but argues they miss the bigger picture.

Here's how to eliminate:

🔴 Option 1 -> definition-error -> just defines what a "bald statement" is, doesn't capture what the author is communicating by telling us to think beyond qualifications

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> captures author's main point: yes, there are caveats, but the core statement remains true at a fundamental level

🔴 Option 3 -> scope-error -> author isn't talking about "free reign to musical expressions" - that's not mentioned anywhere in the passage

🔴 Option 4 -> definition-error -> again just defining terms, not explaining the author's communication. Also wrong - the author admits qualifications do exist, they're just not the main point

The author is saying: Don't get caught up in the details and exceptions - the big truth still stands.

questions.question_text: In the first paragraph of the passage, what are the two "characterisations" that are seen as overlapping but not congruent?

options.label: A
options.text: "individuals" and "social structures".

options.label: B
options.text: "academic disciplines" and "institutions".

options.label: C
options.text: "an arena of thought" and "academic disciplines".

options.label: D
options.text: "the philosophy of the social sciences" and "a set of social institutions".

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "We begin with the emergence of the philosophy of the social sciences as an arena of thought and as a set of social institutions. The two characterisations overlap but are not congruent. Academic disciplines are social institutions."

Step-by-step thinking process:

The author describes philosophy of social sciences in two ways -> these are the "two characterisations" -> first as "arena of thought" -> second as "set of social institutions" -> then clarifies that "academic disciplines are social institutions" -> this connects the dots -> arena of thought = academic disciplines -> set of social institutions = institutions.

So the two characterisations that overlap but aren't congruent are: academic disciplines and institutions.

Option elimination process:

🔴 Option 1 -> context-shift -> "individuals" and "social structures" come later when explaining what institutions do (link individuals into structures), not the two characterisations mentioned at start

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> captures exactly what author means: philosophy of social sciences can be seen as academic disciplines OR as institutions, and these overlap but aren't identical

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> only gives us one actual characterisation ("arena of thought") but pairs it with "academic disciplines" which is the same thing, not the second characterisation

🔴 Option 4 -> scope-error -> tries to make "philosophy of social sciences" itself one of the characterisations, but that's what's being characterised, not how it's being characterised

The key insight: arena of thought = academic disciplines, so the real comparison is between academic disciplines and institutions.

questions.question_text: All of the following inferences from the passage are false, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: the institution of friendship cannot be found in the institution of joint-stock companies because the first is an informal institution, while the second is a formal one.

options.label: B
options.text: "natural language" refers to that stage of language development where no conscious human intent is evident in the formation of language.

options.label: C
options.text: institutions like the family, rituals, governance, economy, and the military are natural and cannot be consciously modified.

options.label: D
options.text: as concepts, "culture" and "tradition" have no analytical, explanatory or expository power, especially when they are treated in isolation.

questions.explanation_text:
The key is to match each option against what the passage actually says, not what seems logical.

From passage: "Natural languages are typical examples of what Ferguson called 'the result of human action, but not the execution of any human design'"

This tells us natural languages happened through human actions but weren't planned -> they developed without conscious intent -> Option 2 looks right.

Let's check the others to be sure:

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> says friendship "cannot be found in" joint-stock companies just because one is informal and one is formal. But passage says institutions can have "mixed variants" - so informal elements can exist within formal institutions.

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> matches exactly what passage says about natural languages being "result of human action, but not execution of human design" -> means no conscious intent in their formation.

🔴 Option 3 -> contradicts passage -> says these institutions "cannot be consciously modified" but passage clearly states "In their present incarnations, however, they are very much the product of conscious attempts to mould and plan them."

🔴 Option 4 -> contradicts passage -> says culture and tradition have "no analytical, explanatory or expository power" but passage says they "are analytically isolated for explanatory or expository purposes" -> meaning they DO have such power.

The confusion students face: Options 1 and 4 might seem reasonable at first glance, but they misread what the passage actually says about mixed institutions and the purpose of isolating culture/tradition.

questions.question_text: "Consider the fact that the stock exchange and the black market are both market institutions, one formal one not." Which one of the following statements best explains this quote, in the context of the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: The stock exchange and the black market are examples of how, even within the same domain, different kinds of institutions can co-exist.

options.label: B
options.text: The stock exchange and the black market are both dependent on the market to survive.

options.label: C
options.text: The stock exchange and the black market are both organised to function by rules.

options.label: D
options.text: Market instruments can be formally traded in the stock exchange and informally traded in the black market.

questions.explanation_text:
Let us trace the author's logic in the passage.

The author is explaining that institutions can be formal or informal -> then gives examples -> stock exchange (formal) and black market (informal) are both market institutions -> this shows different types can exist in the same area.

From passage: "There are some institutions that come in both informal and formal variants, as well as in mixed ones. Consider the fact that the stock exchange and the black market are both market institutions, one formal one not."

Author's thought process -> institutions have different forms -> some formal, some informal -> need examples -> both stock exchange and black market deal with markets -> but one follows official rules (formal) while other doesn't (informal) -> this proves different types can exist together in same domain.

Let's check each option against what the quote is actually demonstrating:

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures the main point that different institutional types (formal vs informal) can exist within the same domain (market institutions)

🔴 Option 2 -> irrelevant -> talks about dependency on markets, but the quote isn't about survival or dependency - it's about showing formal vs informal distinction

🔴 Option 3 -> misses the point -> says both are organized by rules, but that's wrong - black market specifically doesn't follow formal rules, that's why it's informal

🔴 Option 4 -> scope-error -> focuses only on trading mechanisms rather than the broader institutional point about formal vs informal coexistence

The confusion students might have: Options 3 and 4 sound reasonable because they mention both institutions. But remember - the author's goal is to show the formal/informal distinction, not explain how they operate.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements best represents the essence of the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: Language is the fundamental formal institution for social life and for science.

options.label: B
options.text: It is usual in social thought to treat culture and tradition as different from institutions.

options.label: C
options.text: The stock exchange and the black market are both market institutions.

options.label: D
options.text: Institutions are structures that serve to coordinate the actions of individuals.

questions.explanation_text:
The passage keeps coming back to what institutions ARE and what they DO. The author spends most time defining institutions and their coordinating function.

From passage: "Let us straddle all these versions and present institutions very generally as structures that serve to coordinate the actions of individuals."

From passage: "My view is that institutions are all those social entities that organise action: they link acting individuals into social structures."

The author's main point -> Institutions exist to coordinate people's actions -> This is repeated multiple times -> All examples (language, markets, culture) support this central idea.

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> Language is discussed as one example of an institution, but calling it "fundamental formal" overstates its role. The passage says language can be both formal AND informal.

🟠 Option 2 -> context-shift -> This mentions what is "usual in social thought" but the author actually disagrees with this usual view. He says culture and tradition ARE subsets of institutions.

🟠 Option 3 -> scope-error -> This is just a specific example used to show formal vs informal institutions. It's not the main point of the entire passage.

🟢 Option 4 -> captures the essence perfectly -> This is the author's core definition that everything else in the passage supports. All examples (language, markets, culture) are used to show how institutions coordinate actions.

The elimination key: When looking for essence, ignore specific examples and look for the overarching concept that ties everything together.

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. From chemical pollutants in the environment to the damming of rivers to invasive species transported through global trade and travel, every environmental issue is different and there is no single tech solution that can solve this crisis.
  2. Discourse on the threat of environmental collapse revolves around cutting down emissions, but biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse are caused by myriad and diverse reasons.
  3. This would require legislation that recognises the rights of future generations and other species that allows the judiciary to uphold a much higher standard of environmental protection than currently possible.
  4. Clearly, our environmental crisis requires large political solutions, not minor technological ones, so, instead of focusing on infinite growth, we could consider a path of stable-state economies, while preserving markets and healthy competition.
questions.explanation_text:
Step-by-step thought process:

First,we need to find the opening sentence that introduces the main topic -> Sentence 2 talks about environmental discourse and introduces the key problem (biodiversity loss has many causes).

Next, we look for elaboration -> Sentence 1 gives specific examples of those "myriad and diverse reasons" (pollutants, dams, invasive species) and concludes "no single tech solution."

Thenwe need the transition -> Sentence 4 picks up on "no single tech solution" and argues for "large political solutions, not minor technological ones."

Finally, the conclusion -> Sentence 3 gives a specific example of what those political solutions would look like (legislation for future generations).

From passage: "biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse are caused by myriad and diverse reasons" connects to "From chemical pollutants... every environmental issue is different"

The flow is: Problem introduction -> Examples -> Solution type needed -> Specific solution

Key connections to spot:

🟢 2→1: "myriad and diverse reasons" gets examples in sentence 1

🟢 1→4: "no single tech solution" connects to "large political solutions, not minor technological ones"

🟢 4→3: Political solutions idea gets specific with "legislation" example

Correct sequence: 2-1-4-3

The answer 2143 follows this logical progression from problem identification to specific solutions.

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. The trajectory of cheerfulness through the self is linked to the history of the word 'cheer' which comes from an Old French meaning 'face'.
  2. Translations of the Bible into vernacular languages, expanded the noun 'cheer' into the more abstract 'cheerful-ness', something that circulates as an emotional and social quality defining the self and a moral community.
  3. When you take on a cheerful expression, no matter what the state of your soul, your cheerfulness moves into the self: the interior of the self is changed by the power of cheer.
  4. People in the medieval 'Canterbury Tales' have a 'piteous' or a 'sober' cheer; 'cheer' is an expression and a body part, lying at the intersection of emotions and physiognomy.
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Look for the opening sentence -> needs to introduce the main concept without assuming prior knowledge

Step 2: Find the chronological order -> medieval times come before Bible translations

Step 3: Look for connecting words that link sentences together

From passage: "When you take on a cheerful expression, no matter what the state of your soul, your cheerfulness moves into the self"

Thought process:

Sentence 3 introduces the basic concept -> doesn't assume we know anything about "cheer" yet

Sentence 1 connects with "trajectory of cheerfulness through the self" -> builds on what 3 just said

Sentence 4 gives medieval examples -> chronologically comes first in history

Sentence 2 talks about Bible translations expanding the meaning -> comes after medieval times

🟢 Correct sequence (3142):

  • Starts with concept introduction (3)
  • Links to historical trajectory (1)
  • Provides earlier historical examples (4)
  • Shows later development through translations (2)

Wrong sequences would:

🔴 Start with sentence 1 or 4 -> assumes knowledge we don't have yet

🔴 Put sentence 2 before 4 -> puts later historical development before earlier examples

🔴 Break the logical connection between 3 and 1 -> they work together to set up the main idea

The key is finding the sentence that can stand alone as an opener (sentence 3) and then following the natural chronological and conceptual flow.

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. Women may prioritize cooking because they feel they alone are responsible for mediating a toxic and unhealthy food system.
  2. Food is commonly framed through the lens of individual choice: you can choose to eat healthily.
  3. This is particularly so in a neoliberal context where the state has transferred the responsibility for food onto individual consumers.
  4. The individualized framing of choice appeals to a popular desire to experience agency, but draws away from the structural obstacles that stratify individual food choices.
questions.explanation_text:
Step-by-step thinking process:

Start with the topic introduction -> Look for sentences that introduce the main idea first. Sentence 2 talks about "food is commonly framed through individual choice" - this sounds like an opening statement.

Find continuation signals -> Sentence 4 mentions "individualized framing" which directly connects to sentence 2's "individual choice." This builds on the opening idea.

Look for context words -> Sentence 3 starts with "This is particularly so" which means it's explaining when or why the previous idea happens. It provides context for the individualization.

Find the specific example -> Sentence 1 narrows down to women specifically, giving a concrete example of how this food responsibility plays out.

From passage: "Food is commonly framed through the lens of individual choice" -> "The individualized framing of choice" -> "This is particularly so in a neoliberal context" -> "Women may prioritize cooking because they feel they alone are responsible"

Flow: General concept (2) -> Expansion with critique (4) -> Context explanation (3) -> Specific example (1)

Quick elimination strategy: Look for opening sentences (broad statements without "this," "these," "such") and connecting words ("this is particularly," "the individualized framing").

🟢 Sequence 2431 is correct -> follows logical progression from broad concept to specific example with proper connecting language

The answer flows: Individual choice concept -> Critique of this framing -> Context for why this happens -> Specific example with women

questions.question_text:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide where (option 1, 2, 3, or 4) the following sentence would best fit.

Paragraph: Aage Badhein's USP lies in the ethnographic research that constituted the foundation of its development process. Customizations based on learning directly from potential users were critical to making this self-paced app suitable for both a literate and non-literate audience ___ (1) ___ . The user interface caters to a Hindi- speaking audience who have minimal to no experience with digital services and devices ___ (2) ___ . The content and functionality of the app are suitable for a wide audience. This includes youth preparing for an independent role in life or a student ready to create a strong foundation of financial management early in her life ___ (3) ___ . Household members desirous of improving their family's financial strength to reach their aspirations can also benefit. We piloted Aage Badhein in early 2021 with over 400 women from rural areas ___ (4) ___ . The digital solution generated a large amount of interest in the communities.

Sentence: Most were first-time users of a tablet and a digital app.

options.label: A
options.text: Option 1

options.label: B
options.text: Option 2

options.label: C
options.text: Option 3

options.label: D
options.text: Option 4

questions.explanation_text:
The passage moves from general app features -> target audience -> specific pilot study. The key is finding where this detail about user experience fits most naturally.

From passage: "We piloted Aage Badhein in early 2021 with over 400 women from rural areas ___ (4) ___. The digital solution generated a large amount of interest in the communities."

The sentence "Most were first-time users of a tablet and a digital app" provides crucial context about WHO these 400 women were -> explains WHY the solution generated so much interest.

Think about it: rural women + first-time users + generated large interest = perfect logical sequence

🔴 Option 1 -> context-shift -> comes after talking about literate/non-literate audiences, but the sentence is about experience level, not literacy. Doesn't connect to the flow here.

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> mentions minimal digital experience, so first-time users could fit, but this is still general description of target audience, not about the specific pilot study.

🔴 Option 3 -> irrelevant -> talks about different user types (youth, students, household members). The sentence about first-time users doesn't match this categorization context.

🟢 Option 4 is correct -> provides essential detail about the pilot participants -> explains the background of these 400 rural women -> sets up perfectly why they showed such interest in the digital solution.

The sentence acts as a bridge: pilot with 400 rural women -> most were first-time users -> that's why it generated such interest.

questions.question_text:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide where (option 1, 2, 3, or 4) the following sentence would best fit.

Paragraph: For millennia, ghee has been a venerated staple of the subcontinental diet, but it fell out of favour a few decades ago when saturated fats were largely considered to be unhealthy ___ (1) ___ . But more recently, as the thinking around saturated fats is shifting globally, Indians are finding their own way back to this ingredient that is so integral to their cuisine ___ (2) ___ . For Karmakar, a renewed interest in ghee is emblematic of a return-to-basics movement in India ___ (3) ___ This movement is also part of an overall trend towards "slow food". In keeping with the movement's philosophy, ghee can be produced locally (even at home) and has inextricable cultural ties ___ (4) ___ At a basic level, ghee is a type of clarified butter believed to have originated in India as a way to preserve butter from going rancid in the hot climate.

Sentence: This was years in the making but fast-tracked during the pandemic, when "people started being more mindful about their food", he explained.

options.label: A
options.text: Option 1

options.label: B
options.text: Option 2

options.label: C
options.text: Option 3

options.label: D
options.text: Option 4

questions.explanation_text:
The sentence talks about something being "fast-tracked during the pandemic" when people became "more mindful about food" - this clearly connects to the renewed interest in ghee mentioned in the passage.

From passage: "For Karmakar, a renewed interest in ghee is emblematic of a return-to-basics movement in India"

Key clue: The sentence ends with "he explained" -> this means it's continuing someone's quote. Karmakar was just mentioned before position 3, so "he" = Karmakar.

Thought process: Passage talks about ghee's comeback -> mentions Karmakar's view on renewed interest -> perfect spot to add Karmakar's explanation about when/how this happened (pandemic) -> then continues with broader movement context.

Option Analysis:

🔴 Option 1 -> context-shift -> talks about historical decline of ghee, but our sentence is about recent pandemic trends. Doesn't connect logically.

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> mentions return to ghee, but "he explained" has no clear reference since no specific person mentioned yet.

🟢 Option 3 -> perfect fit -> Karmakar just mentioned, so "he explained" works. "Return-to-basics movement" connects perfectly with "more mindful about food" during pandemic.

🔴 Option 4 -> scope-error -> talks about practical aspects of ghee production, but our sentence is about timing of renewed interest, not production methods.

The "he explained" clearly points to Karmakar from the previous line, and the pandemic explanation fits perfectly with his view on the "return-to-basics movement".

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Several of the world's earliest cities were organised along egalitarian lines. In some regions, urban populations governed themselves for centuries without any indication of the temples and palaces that would later emerge; in others, temples and palaces never emerged at all, and there is simply no evidence of a class of administrators or any other sort of ruling stratum. It would seem that the mere fact of urban life does not, necessarily, imply any particular form of political organization, and never did. Far from resigning us to inequality, the picture that is now emerging of humanity's past may open our eyes to egalitarian possibilities we otherwise would have never considered.

options.label: A
options.text: Contrary to our assumption that urban settlements have always involved hierarchical political and administrative structures, ancient cities were not organised in this way.

options.label: B
options.text: The lack of hierarchical administration in ancient cities can be deduced by the absence of religious and regal structures such as temples and palaces.

options.label: C
options.text: The emergence of a class of administrators and ruling stratum transformed the egalitarian urban life of ancient cities to the hierarchical civic organisations of today.

options.label: D
options.text: We now have the evidence in support of the existence of an egalitarian urban life in some ancient cities, where political and civic organisation was far less hierarchical.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the main idea about ancient cities and what they tell us about political organization.

From passage: "Several of the world's earliest cities were organised along egalitarian lines... Far from resigning us to inequality, the picture that is now emerging of humanity's past may open our eyes to egalitarian possibilities"

The passage makes three key points:

  • Some early cities were egalitarian (equal, no rulers)
  • This shows urban life doesn't require hierarchy
  • This evidence opens new possibilities for us

Elimination Strategy: Look for scope errors (too broad/narrow) and focus on what the passage actually proves vs what it just suggests.

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> says all ancient cities weren't hierarchical, but passage says only "several" were egalitarian

🔴 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> focuses only on temples/palaces missing but ignores the bigger point about egalitarian possibilities

🔴 Option 3 -> context-shift -> talks about transformation from ancient to modern times, but passage doesn't discuss this change

🟢 Option 4 is correct -> captures all key elements: evidence exists, some ancient cities, egalitarian life, less hierarchical organization

Why students get confused between Options 1 and 4:

Both mention ancient cities without hierarchy. But Option 1 says this was true for all ancient cities ("ancient cities were not organised this way"), while the passage clearly says only "several" were egalitarian. Option 4 correctly says "some ancient cities" and emphasizes we now have evidence (not just assumptions) supporting this.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Today, many of the debates about behavioural control in the age of big data echo Cold War-era anxieties about brainwashing, insidious manipulation and repression in the 'technological society'. In his book Psychopolitics, Han warns of the sophisticated use of targeted online content, enabling 'influence to take place on a pre-reflexive level'. On our current trajectory, "freedom will prove to have been merely an interlude." The fear is that the digital age has not liberated us but exposed us, by offering up our private lives to machine-learning algorithms that can process masses of personal and behavioural data. In a world of influencers and digital entrepreneurs, it's not easy to imagine the resurgence of a culture engendered through disconnect and disaffiliation, but concerns over the threat of online targeting, polarisation and big data have inspired recent polemics about the need to rediscover solitude and disconnect.

options.label: A
options.text: The role of technology in influencing public behaviour is reminiscent of the manner in which behaviour was manipulated during the Cold War.

options.label: B
options.text: With big data making personal information freely available, the debate on the nature of freedom and the need for privacy has resurfaced.

options.label: C
options.text: The notion of freedom and privacy is at stake in a world where artificial intelligence is capable of influencing behaviour through data gathered online.

options.label: D
options.text: Rather than freeing us, digital technology is enslaving us by collecting personal information and influencing our online behaviour.

questions.explanation_text:
The passage talks about two big ideas that students often miss when they read too fast.

From passage: "Today, many of the debates about behavioural control in the age of big data echo Cold War-era anxieties about brainwashing, insidious manipulation and repression"

The passage starts by connecting current big data debates -> old Cold War fears. Then it explains what's happening now with our personal data being collected and used to influence us.

From passage: "concerns over the threat of online targeting, polarisation and big data have inspired recent polemics about the need to rediscover solitude and disconnect"

This shows the debates are happening now because of big data issues -> people are discussing freedom and privacy again.

Here's how to eliminate wrong options quickly:

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> Only talks about Cold War comparison but completely ignores the main point about big data and current privacy debates. Too narrow - misses half the passage.

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> Gets both parts right: "big data making personal information freely available" + "debate on freedom and privacy has resurfaced" (connecting to those Cold War anxieties mentioned at the start)

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> Mentions freedom, privacy, and AI influence correctly but misses the key connection to Cold War-era debates that the passage opens with. Students often pick this because it sounds comprehensive.

🟠 Option 4 -> overstates -> Makes it sound like we're definitely "enslaved" when the passage is more about debates and concerns about what might happen. Too strong and misses the "resurfaced debate" angle.

The trap many students fall into is picking Option 3 or 4 because they focus on the scary AI stuff. But the passage is really about how old fears are coming back because of new technology - that's exactly what Option 2 captures with "resurfaced."

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

There's a common idea that museum artworks are somehow timeless objects available to admire for generations to come. But many are objects of decay. Even the most venerable Old Master paintings don't escape: pigments discolour, varnishes crack, canvases warp. This challenging fact of art world life is down to something that sounds more like a thread from a morality tale: inherent vice. Damien Hirst's iconic shark floating in a tank entitled The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living is a work that put a spotlight on inherent vice. When he made it in 1991, Hirst got himself in a pickle by not using the right kind of pickle to preserve the giant fish. The result was that the shark began to decompose quite quickly its preserving liquid clouding, the skin wrinkling, and an unpleasant smell wafting from the tank.

options.label: A
options.text: Artworks may not last forever; they may deteriorate with time, and the challenge is to slow down their degeneration.

options.label: B
options.text: Museums have to guard timeless art treasures from intrinsic defects such as the deterioration of paint, polish and canvas.

options.label: C
options.text: Museums are left with the moral responsibility of restoring and preserving the artworks since artists cannot preserve their works beyond their life.

options.label: D
options.text: The role of museums has evolved to ensure that the artworks are preserved forever in addition to guarding and displaying them.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the main message about museum artworks and what challenge they face.

From passage: "There's a common idea that museum artworks are somehow timeless objects available to admire for generations to come. But many are objects of decay."

The passage starts by breaking a myth -> artworks are NOT timeless -> they actually decay naturally. This happens because of "inherent vice" -> the materials themselves cause problems over time.

The author gives two clear examples:

  • Old Master paintings -> pigments change color, varnishes crack, canvases bend
  • Hirst's shark -> decomposed because of wrong preservation method

Key insight: The passage focuses on the natural fact that artworks decay, not on who should fix this problem.

Now let's check each option:

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures the core message that artworks naturally deteriorate and it's challenging to slow this down. Doesn't blame anyone or assign responsibility.

🔴 Option 2 -> contradicts passage -> calls artworks "timeless treasures" when the passage specifically says they're NOT timeless. Also focuses only on museums' duty.

🔴 Option 3 -> scope-error -> shifts focus to "moral responsibility" and artists vs museums. The passage isn't about responsibility - it's about the natural fact of decay.

🔴 Option 4 -> contradicts passage -> says "preserved forever" when the passage shows artworks cannot be preserved forever due to inherent vice.

Student confusion: You might think options 2, 3, 4 are correct because they mention preservation. But the passage isn't about solutions or who should preserve -> it's about the reality that artworks naturally decay.
